summary: Kayti Burt argues that concert films are becoming central to pop music fandom as live tickets grow costlier and harder to get. Drawing on Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour, BTS's Yet to Come, and Beyoncé's Renaissance film, she says films widen access and still deliver community and belonging. She uses her own experience seeing Yet to Come both live in Busan and in cinemas, and argues that in-person attendance should not define a 'bigger' fan.
one_line: Concert films like Taylor Swift's Eras Tour and BTS's Yet to Come make pop fandom more accessible, affordable and inclusive than increasingly costly live tours.
key_facts: Concert tickets are more expensive than ever due to inflation, Ticketmaster's monopolistic practices, and increased demand after COVID-related touring delays.
Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour is an almost three-hour filmed version of her ongoing tour and is now the highest-grossing concert film of all time.

Pitchfork reported in July that the average ticket cost for the North American leg of Swift's Eras Tour was $3,801, a 2,321% increase from her 2018 Reputation Stadium Tour, where the average resale price was $157.
Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour movie tickets are $19.89 for adults.
BTS released a filmed version of their 'Yet to Come' concert in February; the concert was a one-night-only show for 50,000 fans in Busan, South Korea.
The Yet to Come concert film made more than $50 million worldwide, even though the show had been streamed on Weverse to a reported 49 million fans.
Yet to Come will stream on Amazon Prime Video starting Nov. 9.
At the Busan show, the 3,000-strong standing areas got intense as fans pushed toward the stage, prompting BTS to alter plans to come down into the audience for their 2018 hit 'IDOL.'
Burt attended Yet to Come both in person and in cinemas, arriving at the theater just 20 minutes before showtime and watching with friends, lightsticks and a BT21 Tata headband.
The film gave Burt a closer view of the choreography and the BTS members' interaction than she had in person, though she missed the freedom to choose where to look on the stage.
Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé hits theaters in December.
Burt argues that attending in person does not make someone a bigger fan; it reflects luck and privilege, and concert films are 'leveling the field.'
